This conjecture remains open, but Demaine et al. context: Better-than-worst-case optimality. There are many notions for better-than-worst-case complexity, and a long publication history. All these approaches share a common theme: if the worst-case running time of an algorithm is defined as the maximum over all possible input instances, can we instead derive lower bounds from the input instance? The strictest interpretation of this idea is (true) instance optimality. An algorithm A is instance-optimal if there exists a constant c such that, for all sufficiently large input instances I and for all algorithms A′ , we have Running-Time(A, I) ≤ c·Running-Time(A′ , I). Perhaps the most famous instance-optimality conjecture is due to Sleator and Tarjan [23], who proposed that there exists a constant c and a BST algorithm A such that, for every sufficiently long sequence I of predecessor queries, the total running time Running-Time(A, I) of answering all queries in I satisfies Running-Time(A, I) ≤ c · Running-Time(A′ , I) for every other BST algorithm A′ . This conjecture remains open, but Demaine et al. [7, FOCS’04] showed a BST algorithm A that is O(log log n)-instance-competitive: Formally, they showed that, for any sufficiently long sequence I of BST queries and every other BST A′ , Running-Time(A, I) ≤ O(log log n) · Running-Time(A′ , I). True instance optimality is provably unattainable. Consider the family of quadratic-time algorithms {Ai,j } that perform all pairwise comparisons of elements in I in arbitrary order, where Ai,j starts by comparing I[i] and I[j]. For any algorithm A and constant c, there exists an input I and pair (i, j) such that I[i] = I[j] is the only duplicate and, after c comparisons, A has not yet compared I[i] and I[j]. However, Ai,j finds the duplicate after one comparison. In fact, this construction shows that no o(n log n)-instance-competitive algorithm can exist: for any algorithm, there exists an input I and pair (i, j) such that I[i] = I[j] is the only duplicate, and after log(n!) − 1 comparisons, A cannot certify whether I[i] < I[j], I[i] > I[j], or I[i] = I[j]. Yet, Ai,j terminates after one comparison. This calls for a notion of optimality that is more fine-grained than worst-case, but coarser than instance optimality. Output-optimality. Fix some algorithmic problem and a value k, and denote by In,k all inputs of size n that have an output of size k. For a fixed algorithm A and integer pair (n, k), we define the output-sensitive running time as Output(A, n, k) := maxI∈In,k Running-Time(A, I). We say that an algorithm A is output-optimal if there exists a constant c such that, for all k and sufficiently large n, we have, for all A′ , Output(A, n, k) ≤ c · Output(A′ , n, k). A classical result is the O(n log k)-time convex hull algorithm by Kirkpatrick and Seidel [17]. A related but stronger notion is order-oblivious optimality, a term proposed by Afshani, Barbay, and Chan [1, FOCS’09]. Let Π(I) denote all permutations of I. For an algorithm A and input I, we define the order-oblivious running time as Order(A, I) := ′max Running-Time(A, I ′ ). I ∈Π(I) An algorithm A is order-oblivious optimal if for a constant c, for all sufficiently large I, Order(A, I) ≤ c · Order(A′ , I), for all algorithms A′ . [1] proved that the algorithm in [17] is optimal in this model. Note that this notion of optimality implies output-optimality.
